title: Why do big ticket sales crash?

scenes.heading: Why do big *ticket sales* crash?
scenes.subheading: From 500 seats to millions of fans
scenes.narration: In 2022, a huge tour's presale overwhelmed the ticket site. So how would you design ticket sales? Like a real project: start with something simple that works, and fix it only when it breaks.

scenes.caption: a local band · a few hundred fans over a day
scenes.narration: Start small: a local band, five hundred seats, and a few hundred fans buying over a whole day.

scenes.title: What it must do
scenes.narration: Before drawing anything, ask what it must do, and how well. It must show the free seats, and let a fan buy one. And it must never sell a seat twice, and answer in under a second. For now: five hundred seats, a few hundred fans.

items.text: A fan *picks a seat and buys it*
Now: *500 seats*, a few hundred fans

scenes.title: The simple version
scenes.narration: The simple version is three pieces. Fans open the site and pick a seat. The backend is everything on your server; its API is the door the site calls. It checks the seat is free and marks it sold. And the database keeps every seat with its status.

scenes.title: Need anything else?
scenes.narration: With a few hundred fans spread over a day, that's enough. No queue, no cache, no extra servers. This version works, and you could ship it today.

note.text: Extra piece = *one more thing to break*

scenes.caption: two fans click A12 at the same moment
scenes.narration: But what happens when two fans click the same seat at the same moment?

scenes.title: What breaks
scenes.narration: Both requests ask the database: is A12 free? Both get yes. Both mark it sold. Now two people have a ticket for one seat. That's a race condition: the check and the write were two separate steps.

scenes.title: One atomic step
scenes.narration: The fix: make the check and the write one step, an atomic update. The backend tells the database: mark A12 sold, only if it's still free. The first request wins. The second changes zero rows, so that fan loses and picks another seat. That's the price of never selling twice.

scenes.title: Four seats together
scenes.narration: Fans rarely buy one seat; they want four together. Sell them one by one, and the fan can end up with half a group. So sell all four in one transaction: all or nothing. The price: those rows stay locked a little longer, so other fans wait.

scenes.caption: between picking a seat and paying
scenes.narration: Next problem: paying isn't instant. Between picking a seat and finishing the payment, a fan needs a few minutes.

scenes.title: Hold the seat
scenes.narration: So you don't sell the seat at the click: you hold it. The seat goes from free to held, with an expiry time, while the fan pays. When the payment goes through, it becomes sold.

scenes.title: When they walk away
scenes.narration: And if the fan closes the tab? A small job checks for expired holds every minute and frees those seats. The price: a held seat is blocked for everyone else. A long hold blocks seats; a short one makes fans lose them mid-payment.

scenes.title: Paid, but too late
scenes.narration: The fan pays through an outside payment provider, the company that charges the card. They pay in the last second, the hold expires, and another fan takes the seat. So confirm the sale only if the hold is still theirs; if not, refund. The price: that fan is charged, then refunded.

note.text: Confirm *only if the hold is yours*

scenes.title: Charged twice
scenes.narration: Say the backend crashes right after charging, before marking the seat sold. The retry must not charge again. So every payment carries an idempotency key. Analogy: a receipt number. Show it twice, and the provider returns the same receipt, not a second charge. The price: the provider remembers each key.

scenes.caption: total system requests · 2022 presale · 4× its previous peak (Ticketmaster)
scenes.narration: Remember that 2022 presale? It got three and a half billion requests: four times the ticket company's previous peak. What happens to our design?

scenes.title: What breaks now
scenes.narration: Everybody arrives in the same minute, fans and bots, and keeps hitting refresh. The backend runs out of capacity. The database is flooded with seat checks. Some fans can even lose the seats in their cart.

note.text: Goal: *stay up*, still never sell twice

scenes.title: The numbers
scenes.narration: That total doesn't tell us how fast, so let's size an example. A hundred thousand fans refreshing twenty times a minute make about thirty-three thousand requests per second. That's the peak. Most of it is reads: people looking at the seat map. Buying is a small part, fighting for fixed seats.

scenes.title: Scale out
scenes.narration: The first move any engineer makes: scale out. The backend is stateless, meaning it keeps nothing between requests, so you can run many copies. A load balancer in front spreads the traffic across them.

scenes.title: Cache what people look at
scenes.narration: Most of that traffic is people looking, not buying. So serve it from a CDN, servers close to the fans that keep a copy. The price: a few seconds of lag, so a fan may click a seat that's gone. The one-step write still decides who gets it.

note.text: Map can lag: *some click a gone seat*

scenes.title: Where it still breaks
scenes.narration: But every purchase still ends in the same database, which is stateful: it holds the seats. You can add servers, but you can't add seats. The price of scaling out: more machines, still one database. The bottleneck moved: a flood of writes, all queuing on the same rows.

scenes.title: Why not shard?
scenes.narration: Why not split the database into shards? Splitting by event helps with many events, but one huge event is a single hot spot: everyone fights for the same rows. And a read replica, a copy for reading, can't take the purchase: seat writes go to one place.

scenes.title: The waiting room
scenes.narration: Put a waiting room in front. Before the sale, everyone waits on a simple page. At the start, each fan gets a random place in line, so arriving early doesn't help. Then you let people in at the rate your database can handle. The price: some fans wait.

note.text: Instead of error pages: *a fair line*
Let in *what the database can take*

scenes.title: A pass to get in
scenes.narration: But a fan could skip the line by going straight to the load balancer. So each fan who's let in gets a signed token: a pass nobody can fake. The servers check it on every request. No token, no shopping.

note.text: Signed token = a pass nobody can fake

scenes.title: And the bots
scenes.narration: One more enemy: bots. A script can open thousands of sessions and grab seats in milliseconds. So many big sales ask fans to register first and cap tickets per person. They also slow any account that acts too fast. The price: sign-up friction, and limits that real fans hit too.

scenes.title: The room is a target too
scenes.narration: The waiting room is a target too. Serve it as a simple static page from the CDN, so it can take the crowd. Make the token expire after a few minutes and tie it to one fan. And give each fan one place in line, however many tabs they open.

scenes.title: The full flow
scenes.narration: Fans browse the seat map from the CDN, wait in the room, and get in with a token. The load balancer sends them to any copy of the backend, which holds the seat in one atomic step. They pay, and the seat becomes sold. Expired holds go back on sale.

scenes.title: The path
scenes.narration: Each piece came from a real problem, and each has a price. Two clicks: an atomic update, and the loser picks again. Payment: a hold, and blocked seats. Millions: copies and a CDN, still one database. The line: some fans wait. A local band never needs copies, a CDN or a waiting room. Random line, or first come, first served?

points.text: Two clicks → *atomic update* · loser picks again
The line → *waiting room* · some fans wait
A local band → *the first version is enough*

scenes.cta: Random line or first come, first served?

scenes.title: Before you go
scenes.narration: Before you go: tell me in the comments how you'd make the line fair, and which system I should design next. If this helped, a like and a subscribe help the channel a lot.

notes: Ticketmaster's own explanation (Nov 19, 2022) of the Eras Tour Verified Fan onsale (Nov 15): 3.5 million pre-registrations, "3.5 billion total system requests – 4x our previous peak", a "staggering" number of bot attacks plus fans without codes, about 15% of interactions with issues (including passcode validation errors that made some fans lose tickets in their carts). It is a total with no period given, not a rate: 3.5 billion at 33,000 per second would take about 29 hours. The 33,000 per second in the video is our own example.

Requirements are the contract. "Never sell a seat twice" is a hard rule (consistency over availability for the write path); "under 1 second" is a target we state, not a measured number; "stay up on sale day" is the requirement the big day breaks. Say them before drawing anything, because every later piece is judged against them.

The atomic step is a conditional update: UPDATE seats SET status='sold' WHERE id='A12' AND status='free', then check the affected row count. In PostgreSQL (Read Committed) the second UPDATE waits for the first, then re-checks its WHERE on the new row version and changes zero rows (in Repeatable Read it would fail with a serialization error instead). Alternatives: a row lock (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) inside a transaction, or a version column (optimistic locking). The same waiting is why many writers on the same rows queue up inside the database (scene 20); no writes-per-second figure is claimed because there is no source for one.

Alternatives an interviewer may raise. A queue with workers: the fan needs an immediate yes or no, and the waiting room is already the queue in front of the system. A bigger database: it raises the ceiling, but the same rows still serialize the writes, so it only delays the wall. Authorize-then-capture and sharding by section are covered in their own notes.

Group purchases: sell the seats in one transaction, all or nothing. When several buyers lock overlapping seats, lock them in a consistent order (for example sorted by seat id) to avoid deadlocks. The price is that the rows stay locked a little longer, so other buyers wait.

Holds: a held_until timestamp on the seat (reads treat expired holds as free), or a key with a time-to-live in Redis. The expiry job keeps the data clean. The hold length is a product decision (often a few minutes): too long and seats are blocked for nothing, too short and fans lose the seat while they are typing the card.

Payment races: store who holds the seat and until when (held_by, held_until). Confirm with a conditional update (sold WHERE held_by = this fan AND held_until > now). If the hold was lost while the payment was processing, refund. Many sites also extend the hold while a payment is in progress. Another option: authorize first and capture after the seat is confirmed; the money is only reserved for a few days, so it avoids the refund, at the cost of more states to manage and an authorization that can expire.

Payments are asynchronous too: providers confirm with webhooks that can arrive late or twice, so deduplicate by event id. Use an idempotency key per payment attempt: Stripe (API v1: Idempotency-Key header, keys pruned after at least 24 hours), Adyen (keys valid 7 to 14 days) and PayPal (PayPal-Request-Id; not every API supports it) document it. A retry must arrive inside that window. Store the key with the order before calling the provider, so the retry reuses the same key. Add a reconciliation job that compares payments with seats to catch the leftovers (charged but not sold, or sold but not charged).
Why a sequence diagram for the race and for the double charge: both bugs live in the order and timing of messages, which boxes and arrows cannot show.

Capacity: 100,000 fans x 20 refreshes per minute = about 33,000 requests per second; this is an illustrative example, not Ticketmaster's data. The point is the ratio: almost all requests are reads (cacheable), while the writes compete for a fixed set of seats. Size for the peak, not the average.

Scaling out works because the backend is stateless: any copy can serve any request, so a load balancer can spread traffic with no sticky sessions. Session or cart state lives in the database (or a shared cache), not in the server's memory. The price: more machines to run and keep identical, and still one database.

The seat map is read-heavy: serve it from a CDN or a cache with a short TTL (seconds). Showing a seat as free for a second after it was taken is acceptable because the conditional write is the source of truth; the fan just gets 'taken, pick another'. That is the price, and it is why the write, not the map, decides.

Why not shard the database? Sharding by event spreads different events, but one huge event is a single hot partition: thousands of buyers fight over the same rows. Splitting by section is possible, but it would split a group of four seats across shards, and a cross-shard transaction is exactly the cost we avoid. A read replica helps the read side too, but it can't take the purchase: writes for a seat must go to one place to stay consistent.

Virtual waiting rooms (for example Queue-it): over-capacity visitors wait on a separate page; for scheduled sales, early visitors are randomized at the start; people are let in at a configured rate and come back with a token that the server validates; signing the token is the standard way to make it unforgeable. A check done only in the browser can be skipped; checks at the server, CDN or load balancer can't.

Why a line and not error pages: rejecting the extra requests with errors means who gets in is random and rewards whoever retries fastest, often bots. A line is predictable, and a random draw at the start removes the advantage of arriving first. Fairness: random order is fair to everyone who arrived before the start; first come, first served rewards the fastest connection, the most tabs, and bots.

Bots: pre-registration (like Verified Fan), CAPTCHAs, rate limits per account and device, purchase limits per person. Only pre-registration is backed by the Ticketmaster page; the rest is common practice. Each one has a cost (friction for real fans, limits that real fans hit too), and none stops a determined bot alone, so they are layered.

Waiting room hardening: serve the room as a static page from a CDN so it does not fall over itself; tokens are signed, short-lived and bound to one fan; one place per account or device so opening ten tabs gives ten chances to nobody. Once inventory hits zero, serve a cached 'sold out' page so the system stops doing seat checks.

General admission (no numbered seats): a counter with an atomic decrement (for example Redis DECR) can replace per-seat rows; the rule is the same, one writer decides and the check and the write are one step.

The price of each piece, in one line: atomic update, a fan loses the race; group sale, rows locked longer; hold, a blocked seat; refund, a late payer is charged then refunded; idempotency key, the provider remembers it; copies, more to run and still one database; CDN, a map a few seconds old; waiting room, some fans wait and it becomes a target; bot limits, friction for real fans.

The dots, the meters and the timer rings are pictures of magnitude, not measurements (the 40 %, 55 % and 100 % are illustrative). Follow-up questions an interviewer may ask: what if the payment provider is down? how long should the hold be? what happens at sold out? how do you test this with a load test before the real sale?

Design a Ticket Sale for Millions of Fans
System Design Interview: Ticket Booking From 500 Seats to Millions
publish.description: In 2022, a huge tour's presale overwhelmed the ticket site. We design ticket sales the way a real project grows: a simple version for a local band, then race conditions, seat holds, payment failures, and a waiting room for millions of fans. Every piece comes with the problem that asked for it and what it costs.
learn: Starting from requirements, and why the simple design is the right start
Race conditions: how two fans buy the same seat, and the atomic update that fixes it
Why sites hold your seat while you pay, and what a hold costs
Payment failures: late payments, refunds and idempotency keys
Scaling out: stateless copies, a load balancer and a CDN
Why the bottleneck moves to the database, and how a waiting room and bot limits protect the sale
extra: Real numbers: Ticketmaster reported 3.5 billion total system requests (4x its previous peak) for the Eras Tour Verified Fan presale in Nov 2022, including bot attacks and fans without codes (business.ticketmaster.com). The 33,000 requests per second figure is our own example, not company data.

Idempotency keys are documented by Stripe, Adyen and PayPal. A conditional update is how PostgreSQL lets only one writer win a row (Read Committed, its default level): the second UPDATE waits, re-checks its condition and changes zero rows.
publish.comment: Random line or first come, first served? Which is fairer, and which system should I design next?
